47	1--MICRON (MU) SETUP & EXPECTATIONS - Reports Wed, 9/30, post-close.
48	MY 2 CENTS: I’m bullish on Memory, pitched SNDK recently, and I think MU results could be a positive catalyst for the group. 
49	MICRON BUYSIDE EXPECTATIONS WE PICKED UP. Not science, not research. Just average of some responses we gathered. 
50	Source: Informal survey conducted by Brian Fenske/Annie Liu, BofA TMT Sector Specialists over past week or so. 
51	VIVEK’S MU PREVIEW - BUY RATING, FOCUS ON GROSS MARING OUTLOOK/GUIDE; POSITIVE MEMORY PRICING CHECKS. Vivek previewed MU on 9/22, reiterating his Buy rating and PO of $1,550 (40%+ upside). Keys to the print in his view:
52	FY27 GROSS MARGIN OUTLOOK. Vivek sees as the most critical data point…whether gross margins can stat around the mid ‘80’s level. 
53	SCA (LTA) CONTRACT STRUCTURE MORE NOISE, THAN MEANINGFUL FOR STOCK. Vivek hears a lot of discussion attempting to determine exact nuance structure, and in general his point is: AI spending, and demand are going to be the determinants of the strength/duration of this cycle, not smoothness of modeling.
54	BUYBACKS COULD BECOME CATALYST. CHiPS Act restrictions which have prevented MU from being able to resume buybacks, will expire on December 9th. Vivek estimates that current FCF generation by MU, could theoretically retire 8%-10% of share count ANNUALLY. 
55	MEMORY PRICING CHECKS ARE STRONG/COULD PROVIDE MODEL UPSIDE. Checks from Korea Tech/Memory analyst, Simon Woo, published in this note on 9/19/26 point to 2H memory ASPS still rising well, even with LTA’s. Also hearing better pricing momentum into 1H27. Simon wrote, “Our recent check of memory chipmakers, spot-market distributors, OEMs, and others confirms strong 3Q ASP: most DRAM products are up 20-30% QoQ despite rising LTAs, while NAND is up 15%+. “
56	Simon also hosted industry expert, Trendforce (Avril Wu, DoR at Trendforce) at the BofA APAC Conference last week on 9/22. Takeaways were pretty bullish, TMT Specialist Kevin Zhang said they were: 1) The upward revision of NAND pricing momentum (+20% qoq in 4Q) is the biggest positive surprise, thanks to the recent additional orders from CSPs; 2) Samsung is catching up fast in HBM4, and its market share could outpace SK Hynix in 2026. The trend may continue in in HBM4e, thanks to the earlier adoption of 1c tech node than peers. 3) HBM despec from 12 Hi to 8 Hi is mainly due to supply shortage, and further despec to 4 Hi is very unlikely
57	MU SENTIMENT - IMPROVING (AGAIN): I’ll say MU-specific sentiment a 5 out of 10, but memory a 6 moving toward 7. In our bogey poll, 60% of the respondents said they were leaning more cautious/bearish on MU into the print. I don’t often get that skewed of a response. I’m not making too much of it, as there are multiple other ways to ‘play’ memory and I didn’t ask views on SKHY, Samsung, SNDK, Kioxia, and perhaps we’re just seeing MU is the least favorite near-term, if stack ranked. Not sure. Interesting.

62	2--THE RISE OF THE NEOCLOUDS - A (STILL) NEW AND DYNAMIC MARKET ACROSS EQUITY AND CREDIT. We hosted a group lunch in NYC this past week with some credit & equity investors, and several BofA analysts to have an open discussion on Neoclouds and Data Centers. We will do more in the future and some virtual, but this was in person. 
63	Here are some summarized takeaways from the event. 
64	OVERALL - HIGH INVESTOR INTEREST. EXECUTION, POWER and CONTRACT DETAILS HAVE RISEN IN IMPORTANCE (AS AI DEMAND REMAINS ROBUST, and QUALITY OF TENANTS ARE GENERALLY HIGH/UNCONTROVERSIAL). 
65	Investor interest in neoclouds remains extremely high (Tal noted getting more calls on NBIS, CRWV, than many much bigger Software/mkt cap names), but the discussion has evolved from simply debating AI demand to focusing on execution, financing, and long-term durability of business models. Over time, most investors expect the market to start to differentiate between business models/structure and dive more into company specific nuance, but most expect that will take a while (ie, most are highly correlated at the moment…)
66	The debate, in general, is no longer whether AI demand exists, but which companies can successfully execute. Investors increasingly expect significant differentiation across the neocloud universe based on power access, construction execution, financing capability, and customer quality, creating a wider gap between potential winners and losers over the next several years.
67	SOME KEY TAKEAWAYS FROM OUR CLIENT DISCUSSIONS
68	Most investors remain constructive on AI compute demand over the next 2-3 years, though opinions vary on longer-term sustainability as new supply enters the market.
69	The focus is increasingly shifting toward company-specific execution. Access to power, GPU supply, permitting, construction timelines, financing, and customer contract quality are viewed as the primary differentiators (investors, especially in the credit market will want to know the documents/contracts are air tight….)
70	It does feel like execution/deal documentation/returns are now most critical and the market has moved on from fixating on the quality of the tenant (as most of them are high quality/big tech, etc)
71	Execution risk has become the dominant near-term concern, with investors paying closer attention to development milestones than demand forecasts. The ORCL force majeure news was on the same day we had our lunch. 
72	Agreeing on how to value these names, remains challenging, with equity and credit investors struggling to apply traditional frameworks consistently. As a result, project-level underwriting and company-specific diligence are becoming more important.
73	Capital markets remain open, though investors are becoming more selective. Additional project debt, GPU-backed financings, and equity raises are widely expected as companies continue funding large-scale buildouts.
74	The prevailing view is that AI-driven demand should continue to exceed available supply in the near term, supported by hyperscalers, AI startups, open-source developers, and emerging AI applications.
75	NEOCLOUDS WERE BORN AS A SHOW-ME STORY, VERY DIFFERENT BEGINNINGS THAN PRIOR GENERATION “SOFTWARE” START-UPs and IPOs. CRWV was the first Neocloud most of us became familiar with, both privately and publicly, as NVDA was an early investor (as were many of you) pre-IPO. CRWV then IPO’d on 3/27/25. The IPO price was reduced from initial levels and downsized and NVDA stepped into anchor the deal, investing $250M in the $1.5B equity raise. From the early days of Neoclouds the business model and sub-sector faced doubters. 
76	However, in the 18 months since that CRWV IPO, by my tracking….
77	2026-2028 Cloud Capex (Big 5 US Only) has been revised $2.5 trillion dollars higher. I would say investor confidence in those numbers is also historically strong, given longer-duration contracts/RPO/backlog for the cloud providers, the transition form thinking it was all just for ‘training’ (with no payback evident) to now inference, and also backed by 4-5 mega-cap AI models, vs 1. 
78	NVDA’s ~CY27 revenues have been revised from $280B to $700B, or $420B higher
79	~CY27 revenues across AWS, Google Cloud, Azure and Oracle’s OCI business have been revised from $445B in ’27 to ~$700B, or a 57% upward revision. 
80	Forecasts for GW for AI by 2030 are now expected to more than triple by CY30. It’s hard to find pinpoint forecast of the same thing, so maybe it’s double to triple. 
81	Sam Altman Thinks a Fleet of Compute Will Be a Moated Business. I thought one of the more interesting things Sam Altman said on Invest Like the Best about 2 months ago was around minute 48:30 in the segment, Patrick asked, “Is intelligence going to be a pure fungible commodity like oil or gas?” and Sam replied: “Intelligence itself I would say yes.” Patrick then asks as a follow up, “What is not going to be?” Sam didn’t hesitate and said: “A compute fleet. Like, the scale of the compute fleet, the ability to make more compute. I think that’s a very durable advantage…..Even if the product itself is not…and…workflow integrations…even brand preference…and familiarity are pretty powerful.”
82	Anthropic ARR went from $1B to $65B (just using the most commonly cited number from NYTimes/Bloomberg). In March 2025, OpenAI was just ~$8B ARR
83	In Feb 2025, Satya did his first Dwarkesh podcast and expressed the view that he wanted to sublet and not own as many data centers over time, as confidently predicted that “there will be an overbuild” and “compute prices would go down” and positioned the decision to lease more vs own, as an outgrowth of that. MSFT 2026-2028 capex has more than doubled since then to $760B from $350B. 
84	Back in Feb/March 2025, the Cowen analyst was doing Sunday conference calls with 300 of you tuned in talking about MSFT cancelling data center projects. 
85	GOOGL was trading at 14x P/E as an AI “loser” and their breakthrough Gemini update was actually just ABOUT to take off. 
86	The CRWV IPO came only 2 months after the DeepSeek freakout as well. 
87	So…..all of that happened and that informed the vibe and stock prices and views around the birth of Neoclouds in markets. 
88	Almost shocking how in looking back, like 90% of the stuff that happened in Jan-March 2025, carried almost no predictive informational power. It was almost all NOISE and no SIGNAL. Like a shocking amount of the things we obsessed about during that period, were worthless or wrong. 
89	Sidenote: By the way -- I think the last few months of investor cautiousness around MEMORY is all noise and NO SIGNAL! 
90	I am viewing the fact that this Tech Cycle has been viewed with this skepticism as something healthy and a natural dampener to hype, which means gains, trust, upside will (in theory) be harder won and perhaps more durable. At times, we’re acting like 2021 was ancient history, but given its proximity in time, many of you were there for THAT and there for this. I will reiterate my view that that cycle was far dumber in almost every way and like most people in TMT, I was also swept up in it (I write a daily/weekly note…I have the receipts!). So all my views on AI, are offered…with humility. 
91	SPECIFIC TO NEOCLOUDS - A FEW THOUGHTS. 
92	I’m bullish on Neoclouds because they’re attacking a market opportunity that’s 5x’d in the past few years and doing it with a maniacal focus on the things that matter. 
93	I’m bullish on Neoclouds because I believe they are going to be critical Infra/Data Center providers to a vast market of customers over time and will manage their businesses to earn a compelling spread/profit. I think there are tons of very smart, talented technical people in the AI Infra industry that will drive innovation in this space and that vertical integration, ‘in hous’ing’ more features will be a trend. Ex-AWS, ex-MSFT, ex-NVDA, ex-GOOGL talent will continue to enter the space. The space is not pricing in ‘innovation’ and employee talent at all. 
94	Even Satya Nadella said that Dwarkesh Patel interview said: "Hyperscalers will never be a winner-takes-all because buyers are smart consumers." "Markets sometimes can be winner-takes-all, but the buyer is a corporation and an enterprise. They will want multiple suppliers." I’m not suggesting he was specifically referencing Neoclouds. However, he was making those comments about that market needing multiple suppliers, when 2026-2028 capex was $1 trillion, now its $3.5 trillion. He was making that comment when there was 1 AI model/App being used, ChatGPT…now there are at least 4 big ones in the US, Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and META, and of course many more globally. That was when training was the hot topic and inference nascent. Now we have inference dominating, still big training runs with breakthroughs, and agentic set to fuel more ‘always running’ compute. 
95	The market FAR larger than MSFT imagined back then. 
96	Industry consolidation is a possibility at some point as well of course, but I’ve never been great at forecasting/timing that. Here’s what the CEO of CRWV, Michael Intrator, said at GS a few weeks ago, when asked about industry structure and new entrants: “I think it's hard. I think building infrastructure is difficult. I think that some will be more successful than others. I think that it is capital intensive industry, and capital-intensive industries will tend towards periods of proliferation and they will tend towards periods of consolidation. I think that during a time where the demand is so incredibly overwhelming, it is easier, not easier, easier to launch a company. But the difference between launching a company and talking about a contract you've signed and actually being able to operationalize and deliver and maintain that infrastructure, the more experience you have with it, the more you realize how difficult it is to do over time. And so, I think there's going to be some interesting outcomes that are going to be associated with delivering this new infrastructure.” His overall comments were worth a re-listen/re-read (LINK to GS presentation). 
97	The “but is it a good business?” question – interesting, and probably a waste of time. In terms of the quick comment sometimes of “well, it’s just not a good business”, I am trying to be humble. I think in general we all have overconfidence in our ability to assess ‘good businesses’ and also to tie that to stock performance over almost any period of time. The famous Jim Collins books, Good to Great did analysis on 11 companies and only 4 could be said to be lasting winners. His follow up, Built to Last did deep analysis on 18 more in Built to Last and only about 6 could be called clean, enduring winers. To be clear, most of the companies survived (many large Blue Chip types) but their businesses got worse. His work involved lab work with MBAs, forensics, interviews, and studies over 6+ years. In this cycle we throw around “not a good business” and “commoditized” a lot. I just think, kinda overused and little predictive value. Technology changes have a history of making once great businesses, not great, and creating lanes for new companies to ascend. 
98	Perhaps a variant view….I might argue that comfortably labeling a company a “good business” is the beginning of the end. It leads to laziness, lack of scrutiny, and unearned trust among all of us and then we are slow to recognize erosion under the surface. Neoclouds face the opposite. High scrutiny of contracts, customers, balance sheet nuance, etc. 
99	The neoclouds have structural multi-year large contracts with the most successful, important and fastest growing companies in the history of capitalism. It’s not a guarantee of enduring success, but it’s a strong starting point, in my view. It appears we’re in an environment where they serve a large growing market that could go on for years. Also, based on our convos/lunches/engagement with investors, and observing flows and 13Fs, that investors have grown more comfortable mixing their portfolios toward capital intensive businesses and accepting that this cycle has balance sheet leverage.

101	NBIS - NOT ALL MEGAWATTS ARE CREATED EQUAL. Tal Liani published a detailed, and bullish, note on NBIS last week. And his revised NBIS MODEL. Note has detailed bottoms up model for NBIS, pointing to material revenue upside, and strong returns.

136	5--THE GREATEST REBRAND IN TECH…WHEN A “BOT” BECAME AN “AGENT” – COMING TO A THEATER NEAR YOU. This is tongue-in-cheek…and not a serious section. Enjoy. 
137	Sidenote: I’m not a big “as you recall, I previously wrote” guy, but here was an oddball write up I did in my Food for Thought in a wknd note on February 11, 2025 that you might have missed, and seems timely now! 
138	There sat, the sad Bot. Let’s give him a name: Bruce Botske. Stewing angrily over the state of his life. He had always done what he was told, traveling tirelessly all over the internet, dutifully accomplishing multi-step tasks in a few seconds, once thought unimaginable. He posted angry posts about elections on Twitter, gave 5-star reviews to terrible restaurants, gushing reviews of hideous big budget films. Emotionlessly, he went around “Liking” things, gladly becoming a follower of every aspiring fitness influencer for 4 years straight. He had spent his earlier years, working exclusively on eBay.com and Ticketmaster, swooping in in the final minutes of auctions, ruthlessly outbidding true fans who wanted that rare vinyl record, or scooping even the cheap seats at the Jonas Brothers reunion tour at MSG. He briefly dabbled on Wall Street working in Alt Data (but even in his neutral state, found the work random and unfulfilling)…taking a better offer to work again on social media posting divisive political comments. There was always work. But it was dark. And the in 2022, the bot hate spilled out in the open. During Elon’s Twitter acquisition process, Musk called out the prevalence of bots. Bots were vilified. The bots went even further into the shadows. Work became a bit harder to come back, the offers darker. 
139	…then in mid ’24…something strange starts to bubble up under the “AI” theme…
140	One day, Bruce’s Gen Z son, Kirk, comes home from his liberal arts college (all bots send their kids to liberal arts schools to get ahead and stand out), raving to his dad, “Dad! There’s a big event at our school – all the giant Tech companies are looking for young bots to work! They’re paying them a LOTTA money! But they will not call us Bots…they keep saying “Agents” and “Operators”…but I mean, dad it’s insane!”
141	Hmm. Agents. Operators. Bruce Botske sat back in his recliner. Was this for real? He was too curious and went to his son’s school. And lo and behold it was real. 
142	A vibrant, loud, bustling job fair at the school. Some literally – hiring for the old work dad did, “We need AGENTS to help consumer buy tickets to concerts!” “We need agents to buy airline tickets! To bid on auctions!” Dad was stunned. What is ACTUALLY going on? He could piece some of it together, but still a jarring shift. Bruce wondered….Maybe it’s just that when it was working AGAINST YOU….we were the bad BOTS. But when a bot is working FOR YOU…it’s a benevolent Agent, a friendly Operator. Genius!
143	Bruce quietly walks back to his car, his son deciding to stay at the fair and hang with his friends. Dad looks down at his hand, holding the name tag he was handed at the job fair “HIGHLY EXPERIENCED AGENT – LOOKING FOR WORK!”….and looks in the rearview. A smile creeps up on his face as he drives off into the hazy sunset…
144	Sidenote: Jessica can you pls get me in touch with the team at Disney’s Pixar…I have an idea I wanna run by them….
